article_title: How States Are Expanding Quality Summer Learning Opportunities
citation: Fitz, J., Woods, J., Duran, N., & McCombs, J. (2025). How states are expanding quality summer learning opportunities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/910.329
title: Quality markers in out-of-school time programming
description: The report enumerates program features associated with positive attendee outcomes in out-of-school time research. For personal and social skills programs: "well-trained staff who deliver instruction focused on building specific skills, active learning opportunities, and positive youth–staff interactions and site climate." For academic-focused programs, it adds "sufficient program duration and student attendance, instruction from certified teachers with content and grade-level experience, and academically rigorous curriculum." States used these markers to shape grant requirements and guidance.
requirements: Programs seeking positive outcomes should incorporate the listed features associated with quality in the research literature
constraints: The markers are associations from prior research (Durlak et al., 2010; Schwartz et al., 2018), not findings tested in this study
target_learners: K-12 youth in summer and out-of-school time programs
target_learning_goals: personal and social skills
academic achievement
examples: States required funded providers to adopt elements of quality programming and issued voluntary guidance referencing these features

citation: Mellor, D. (2021). Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor. Educational Psychologist, 56(2). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3125-5888
title: Open Science Framework and research data repositories as infrastructure for sharing
description: The article describes digital infrastructure that makes open practices possible and easy. End-of-life repositories archive materials "not commonly preserved or rarely published, such as protocols, stimuli, questionnaires, raw data, analytical code". The Open Science Framework (OSF) is an open-source workspace connecting project pages to registries, repositories, and preprint servers, providing persistent, citable, timestamped links so authors need not reorganize materials at project's end. The Re3data registry catalogues repositories, including many supporting restricted access for sensitive data.
requirements: Persistent, unique identifiers (PUIDs) for datasets and instruments; for sensitive data, restricted-access workflows with an ethical check prior to access; when data cannot be shared, code, instruments, and surveys can still be shared
constraints: The article notes that in education research, quick and easy data sharing is particularly challenging, and that complete transparency is sometimes not ethical or legally feasible
target_learners: research lab members managing ongoing projects
target_learning_goals: documenting and preserving research materials
enabling verification and reuse of data and code
examples: The article cites the Re3data catalogue of over 2,000 repositories, over 1,100 offering restricted access, and the Qualitative Data Repository at Syracuse University for ethical sharing of qualitative data

article_title: Harmonic memory signals in the human cerebral cortex induced by semantic relatedness of words
citation: Noguchi, Y. (2024). Harmonic memory signals in the human cerebral cortex induced by semantic relatedness of words. npj Science of Learning, 9:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00221-1
title: Oscillatory resonance/sharing model of semantic integration in verbal working memory
description: The article proposes that each semantic feature of a word is maintained as a neural oscillation at a specific frequency, and that memorizing words sharing a common feature "induces a resonance or sharing of the oscillatory signal across the words, generating a regular EEG waveform" with fewer spectral frequencies. This contrasts with memorizing unrelated words, which produces an irregular waveform "composed of a larger number of frequencies (like white noise)". The alpha-to-beta band (8–30 Hz) carries these harmonic signals, which the author contrasts with theta-gamma coupling models that encode item sequences while keeping items independent.
requirements: Retention of multiple word items in verbal working memory, with alpha-to-beta oscillatory activity over temporal cortex measurable during the retention period
constraints: The author states the model "might be oversimpliﬁed, given that neural underpi nnings of semantic information have been mostly unclear and controversial"

The study did not directly investigate semantic knowledge in long-term memory (mental lexicon); results are interpreted as reflecting the WM process in posterior regions rather than the anterior temporal semantic hub
Results are also consistent with more complex models in which a single feature is recalled as combined signals of multiple frequencies
target_learners: healthy adult humans performing verbal working memory tasks
target_learning_goals: retention and integration of word lists in verbal working memory
semantic chunking of related items
examples: Experiment 1 compared Sem and NonSem trials during delay 5 and found reduced IPI-SD over posterior temporal cortex; Experiment 2's animacy-judgment RSA showed semantically associated words induced similar IPI distributions

target_learning_goals: Assessment of clinical reasoning, communication, professionalism, and professional competencies via oral examination

description: A model derived by the authors from thematic analysis of student interviews (Fig. 2), mapping factors that positively or negatively affect OSCE-related anxiety and performance. As the article states, "the relationship between anxiety and performance appears to be moderated by the sense of self-efficacy." Confidence calms students and improves perceived performance, while being observed, poor interpersonal skills, and theory-practice gaps raise anxiety. It frames the authors' interpretation that self-efficacy may protect performance from stress effects.

citation: Iversen Else Dalsgaard, Wolderslund Maiken Overbeck, Kofoed Poul-Erik, Gulbrandsen Pål, Poulsen Helle, Cold Søren, Ammentorp Jette. (2020). Codebook for rating clinical communication skills based on the Calgary-Cambridge Guide. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02050-3
title: Observation Scheme-12 (OS-12): a 12-item assessment tool for rating clinical communication skills based on the Calgary-Cambridge Guide
description: The OS-12 is an observation-based rating instrument for clinical communication. The article states it "contains 12 items covering the following six domains: initiating the session, gathering information, building the relationship, explanation and planning, providing structure, and closing the session." Each item is rated 0–4 ('Poor' to 'Excellent'), giving an overall score range of 0 to 48 points. In this study it was applied to audio recordings of real outpatient consultations to assess the outcome of communication skills training.
requirements: Raters need "an understanding of the micro-skills as described in the C-CG" before using the OS-12 and codebook, as coding depends on identifying micro-skills.
constraints: The OS-12 did not include every micro-skill from the C-CG (which contains 73 different micro-skills); it reflects the skills prioritized in the specific training course, and the coding tool must be used considering this limitation.
target_learners: Health care providers (medical doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, chiropractors) in clinical communication skills training
target_learning_goals: Clinical communication skills throughout the HCP-patient encounter
examples: Used to rate 51 HCPs' audio-recorded consultations before and after communication skills training at a Danish interdisciplinary outpatient spine clinic in a pre and post design.

title: Retain all OS-12 items and maintain the 5-point scale; use 'not applicable' only for technical recording problems
description: The article recommends keeping the instrument intact despite low-ICC items, arguing "the OS-12 is based on the C-CG and therefore builds on the assumption that every item is essential". It also states "We recommend maintaining the 5-point scale when utilizing the OS-12, as all micro-skills are divided into groups of five", and that the "not applicable" option should be used "only due to technical difficulties" such as recordings that start late or stop early.
requirements: Raters use the full 12-item instrument with the codebook; the 'not applicable' response option is reserved for technical recording problems.
constraints: Low-variance items can still show low ICCs; the authors note the well-known problem of low ICC when items have low scores or variance, though they state this problem was not observed in the present study.
target_learners: Health care providers assessed with the OS-12
target_learning_goals: Reliable assessment of clinical communication skills
examples: In this study no items were coded 'not applicable' when the entire encounter was recorded, and none of the 12 items were excluded.

title: Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) with six stations and seven assessment steps for evaluating infiltration skills
description: Skills were evaluated by an OSCE in which participants circulated through 6 stations, one for each infiltration type (knee via lateral and anterior approach), with 7 minutes per station. Participants were evaluated on "positioning, palpation, identification of the injection site, disinfection and sterility, needle position, aspiration and injection, informing the patient", one point per correct step, plus a 0–10 global rating for proficiency, systematics and completeness. title: Objective structured teaching examination (OSTE) with standardized students for evaluating clinical teachers' feedback skills
description: An OSTE employs standardized students (SSs) to evaluate the teaching skills of clinical teachers or residents, similar to how OSCEs evaluate medical students' clinical skills. Stations present constructed clinical scenarios such as bedside teaching, ambulatory care education, chart writing, and feedback giving, with clear objectives and standards provided for assessment. In this study, a 15-minute feedback-skills station was used, in which a standardized student (played by a resident) reported a case of acute gastric ulcer with bloody stool and abdominal pain, including a family–team conflict, requiring the teacher to give feedback and suggestions. The article notes SSs provide "a highly realistic and low-risk simulated environment in which teachers can practice, experience new teaching techniques and behaviors, and receive direct feedback".

Clear objectives and standards provided for the assessment
constraints: Summative evaluation in this study analyzed only one station (feedback skills)
target_learning_goals: Feedback-giving skills
Teaching skills assessment
Teaching practice in a low-risk environment
examples: The feedback station scenario involved an SS reporting an acute gastric ulcer case with bloody stool, abdominal pain, and a family–medical team conflict, requiring the teacher to give feedback on how to proceed
